catalog_quote: 3.3.2.1. Significance of stress Stress is a significant feature, but it is predictable and thus not phonemic. ... 3.3.2.4. Position of stress Stress position is regular, and its assignment applies uniformly to all words and compounds. Stress assignment can be described most economically by making reference to the moraic structure of the word, and by treating geminated vowels as two morae. Words of one mora, which are all grammatical morphemes (cf. 3.2.4), do not carry stress. In words of two or more morae, primary stress generally falls on the penultimate mora: (3097) ave [1ave] 'send' tele [1tele] 'run' maeva [ma1eva] 'in flight' maafatia [ma?fa1tia] 'sorrowful' ... When the penultimate mora is part of a geminated vowel, stress is distributed evenly over the entire vowel: (3098) taa [1ta?] 'beat' ... uatee [ua1te?] 'noisy' patoo [pa1to?] 'emit booming sound' maamaa [ma?1ma?] 'cheap, li…

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is present verbatim in the Besnier 2000 text we hold at sec. 3.3.2.1/3.3.2.4, printed pp. 613-615, exactly as the locator states; the supporting 'geminated vowels count as two morae' passage (3.3.1) is also there. (2) The source is the standard full reference grammar (662 pp, 2000, Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description) by the language's main describer, with an explicit mora-based stress analysis; the classification 'weight' (penultimate mora, CVV heavy, right edge, secondary stress two morae before primary) follows the text directly. (3) No better or competing stress description was found: Glottolog lists no phonology item for tuva1244 and Crossref shows no Tuvaluan stress/prosody study; nothing open needed downloading, so the list of works to obtain is empty. (4) Status well-sourced; no action.
